framework: In addition to the suite-specific physical models, a complete industrial engineering platform needs shared numerical methods. These methods solve the governing equations, couple different physics, handle realistic geometric domains and quantify numerical and modelling uncertainty.
Numerical discretization and solution methods

The platform should support the finite-element method, finite-volume method, finite-difference method, boundary-element method, spectral-element method, discontinuous Galerkin method, meshfree methods, smoothed particle hydrodynamics, material point method and discrete element method where their physical applications justify them.

For static and nonlinear engineering systems, it should support direct linear solvers, sparse matrix factorization, conjugate gradient methods, generalized minimal residual methods, multigrid algorithms, Newton–Raphson iterations, modified Newton methods, quasi-Newton methods, line-search algorithms, trust-region methods, continuation techniques and arc-length methods.

For transient simulation, it should include explicit Euler, implicit Euler, Runge–Kutta methods, adaptive Runge–Kutta schemes, Newmark-beta, generalized-alpha, Hilber–Hughes–Taylor integration, backward differentiation formulas and implicit–explicit time integration.

For fluid calculations, the appropriate methods should include Godunov-type finite-volume schemes, Roe-type approximate Riemann solvers, HLL and HLLC schemes, MUSCL reconstruction, total variation diminishing schemes, flux limiters, pressure–velocity coupling algorithms, projection methods and volume-of-fluid interface tracking.
Coupled multiphysics simulation

The platform should support fluid–structure interaction, soil–structure interaction, thermal–structural coupling, electrothermal coupling, hydroelasticity, aeroelasticity, poromechanics, mechanical–hydraulic coupling, environmental–structural coupling and coupled structural–economic optimization.

Both monolithic coupling and partitioned iterative coupling should be available when appropriate. Strongly coupled systems should support interface equilibrium, load transfer, displacement continuity, energy consistency, conservation checks and convergence control.
Numerical verification, validation and uncertainty

The platform should incorporate mesh refinement studies, time-step convergence analysis, Richardson extrapolation, Grid Convergence Index methods, method of manufactured solutions, analytical benchmark comparisons, conservation residual checks, nonlinear solver convergence assessment and cross-solver comparisons.

Physical validation should use independent laboratory tests, offshore field measurements, monitoring records, full-scale structural tests, model-scale hydrodynamic experiments and measured geotechnical behaviour where applicable.

Uncertainty and reliability methods should include Monte Carlo simulation, Latin hypercube sampling, first-order and second-order reliability methods, Bayesian inference, Markov chain Monte Carlo, polynomial chaos expansion, stochastic collocation, Gaussian process surrogates, global sensitivity analysis and probabilistic model calibration.
Industry design standards and acceptance models

The platform should separate physical simulation from the design-code checking layer. Depending on the suite and jurisdiction, appropriate references can include ISO offshore and marine standards, API recommended practices, DNV standards and recommended practices, IEC offshore wind requirements, Eurocodes and relevant marine classification rules.

In particular, offshore environmental loading, structural fatigue, submarine pipelines, risers and offshore wind foundations are governed by different technical requirements and assessment methods. The application should identify the exact standard, edition, safety class, load combination and acceptance criteria used for each calculation.
Recommended computational architecture
Engineering project data layer
Geometry, materials, metocean, geotechnics, operating data, costs and boundary conditions
Physical and mathematical model layer
Classical equations, constitutive laws, empirical closures, advanced physics and coupled models
Numerical solver layer
Structural, fluid, geotechnical, thermal, electrical, dynamic and optimization solvers
Coupled engineering analysis layer
16 physical engineering suites exchanging compatible loads, motions, reactions and operating conditions
Suite 17 — Economics
Lifecycle costs, production revenues, reliability costs, investment analysis and design optimization
Verification, validation and reporting
Numerical accuracy, experimental comparisons, uncertainty, compliance, engineering reports and decision support
Important distinctions for software development

Classical equations and models represent established mathematical descriptions of engineering behaviour, including conservation laws, elasticity, beam theory, potential flow, thermodynamics and classical soil mechanics.

Advanced models extend those descriptions through nonlinear material behaviour, large deformation, high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics, multiphase transport, detailed contact mechanics, stochastic loading and coupled multiphysics.

Hybrid models connect two or more appropriate approaches, such as finite-element structural analysis with empirical fatigue correlations, potential-flow hydrodynamics with viscous corrections, or physical asset models with data-driven condition monitoring.

Numerical methods are algorithms used to solve equations. They are not additional physical laws, and using a more sophisticated numerical solver does not automatically make a physical model more accurate.

Industry empirical correlations depend on experimental calibration and specified applicability ranges. They must not be applied universally to geometries, materials or operating conditions outside those ranges without independent justification.

Final engineering position: These 17 suites provide an extensive catalogue of classical, advanced and hybrid methods for a unified offshore engineering platform. However, this catalogue is a model-selection and software-requirements foundation, not evidence that every method is universally applicable or that an implementation is already validated. A credible industrial application must select appropriate formulations for each problem, implement them correctly, demonstrate numerical convergence and validate their predictions against relevant engineering evidence before claiming predictive capability.
integration: Integration of the 17 Suites into One Engineering Simulation Platform

For a comprehensive industrial software application, the suites should not operate as isolated calculation tools. They should exchange validated project data, physical loading conditions, computed reactions, material quantities, operating limits and reliability estimates.

Examples of data exchange between suites

Topside reactions feed jacket analysis; jacket foundation loads feed pile and soil assessments. Foundation stiffness and displacements return to the structural model when coupled analysis is required.
Vessel motions affect line tensions and riser dynamics; line and riser reactions feed back into the vessel motion solution for fully coupled simulations.
Engineering quantities inform project costs; predicted performance and reliability inform operating expenses, production revenue and lifecycle value.

Essential requirements for credible industrial implementation

The inputs and outputs above define the expected data interfaces and engineering deliverables, but a list of inputs and outputs alone does not establish that the corresponding calculation engine is validated.

For industrial credibility, every suite should additionally support defined initial and boundary conditions, appropriate physical and mathematical models, mesh and numerical convergence checks, verification against known solutions, comparison with independent experimental or field measurements, uncertainty quantification and traceable design-code acceptance criteria.
User-supplied data: Information measured, specified or imported by engineers.
Derived data: Quantities calculated from other inputs, such as submerged weight, section properties or equivalent stiffness.
Calibrated parameters: Model coefficients determined using suitable experimental or field datasets.
Simulation results: Numerical predictions generated under a specified model and set of conditions.
Verified and validated results: Outputs whose numerical accuracy and physical predictive capability have been assessed within a documented scope.
Design acceptance results: Pass/fail decisions against the applicable project criteria, with engineering judgment and qualified review where necessary.

Overall: The 17 suites now have a practical industrial input/output specification spanning fixed and floating offshore assets, marine structures, subsea infrastructure, renewable-energy installations, operations and lifecycle economics. They provide a foundation for detailed software requirements, module architecture, data schemas and engineering calculation workflows.

Important engineering implementation considerations
For each of the 17 suites, the software should distinguish between conditions that are physically necessary, optional, analysis-dependent and mutually incompatible.

For example, a fixed offshore platform under static loading does not ordinarily require initial velocity, while a time-domain seismic analysis does. A pipeline hydraulic simulation may require a suitable pressure condition at one end and a flow condition at the other, but prescribing incompatible pressure and flow conditions can overconstrain the numerical problem. A seabed contact model must distinguish between compression-bearing contact and possible uplift separation rather than treating every contact node as permanently fixed.

The software should therefore permit analysis-specific condition sets, including operating conditions, extreme environmental events, installation stages, transient startup and shutdown, accidental loading, damaged conditions and life-extension assessments.

For a credible industrial implementation, each suite should also support consistency checking of input units, validation of geometric compatibility, detection of overconstrained or underconstrained boundaries, equilibrium verification, initialization from a previously converged state, and explicit reporting of the exact initial and boundary conditions used for each simulation.

Taken together, these conditions establish a comprehensive classical engineering framework for configuring the 16 physical simulation suites and the additional Economics suite, without presuming that one generic set of conditions can be applied unchanged to every analysis.
cvv: Common Calibration, Verification and Validation Requirements Across All 17 Suites
For an integrated engineering software platform, individual suite validation is necessary but not sufficient. The full system must also undergo cross-suite verification and validation.
1. Calibration data management

Every calibrated parameter should have a documented physical meaning, unit, admissible range, original source and applicable operating conditions. The calibration record should identify the experimental or field measurements used, measurement uncertainty, calibration method, objective quantities, parameter uncertainty and any observed parameter correlations.

Parameter identifiability should be assessed to establish whether the measurements can meaningfully determine the selected calibration parameters. Where multiple parameter combinations produce equivalent predictions, the uncertainty should be retained rather than presenting the fitted values as unique physical measurements.
Calibration datasets should be separated from independent validation datasets. Data preprocessing, filtering, outlier treatment and measurement corrections should be recorded and reproducible.
2. Numerical and software verification

All numerical solvers should undergo documented regression testing, analytical benchmark testing where suitable solutions exist, and comparison against independently established numerical reference solutions.

Finite-element, finite-volume, finite-difference and other numerical formulations should be tested for spatial convergence, temporal convergence, stability, appropriate conservation properties and correct boundary-condition implementation.

Mesh independence should be assessed using systematic refinement, while recognizing that some nonlinear contact, fracture, localization and turbulence calculations require specialized convergence criteria or regularization.
Transient solvers should be tested for appropriate time-step sensitivity and correct handling of startup, shutdown, changes in loading and transitions between physical regimes.
Nonlinear calculations should be checked for convergence of residuals, equilibrium, solution increments and physically meaningful constraints.
Software verification should include automated unit tests, integration tests, regression tests, numerical precision tests and reproducibility testing across supported computing environments.
3. Physical validation and benchmarking
Validation datasets should be selected to represent the specific physical behaviour and operating range for which the software is intended.

Where possible, the validation programme should include laboratory experiments, physical-model tests, full-scale qualification tests, operational monitoring, offshore field measurements and documented industrial case studies.

The primary assessment quantities should be defined in advance. Depending on the suite, these may include stresses, deflections, natural frequencies, response amplitudes, pressure losses, line tensions, fatigue lives, soil settlement, energy production or project costs.

Model predictions should be compared with measurements using suitable accuracy and uncertainty indicators such as root-mean-square error, mean absolute error, normalized error, bias, correlation measures, confidence intervals and uncertainty coverage.

These statistics should support, rather than replace, physical interpretation. A low average error does not establish acceptability if the model substantially underpredicts critical maximum loads, failure conditions or rare events.
4. Integrated cross-suite verification

The integrated software should be tested for consistent exchange of structural reactions, vessel motions, hydrodynamic loads, foundation stiffness, pipeline and riser forces, installation conditions and economic quantities.

For example, loads transferred from offshore topsides into a jacket should be equal and opposite to the corresponding interface reactions under compatible sign conventions. Foundation displacements should be communicated consistently to supported structures where coupling is required.

Floating structure motion predictions should be compatible with the imposed boundary conditions in mooring and riser calculations. Where tightly coupled dynamics are important, the software should demonstrate convergence of the coupled solution rather than relying solely on sequential data exchange.
Engineering material quantities, inspection requirements, installation durations, operating performance and reliability estimates should transfer consistently into the Economics suite.
5. Uncertainty quantification and reliability
All suites should distinguish measurement uncertainty, uncertain material properties, environmental variability, model-form uncertainty and numerical discretization error.
Sensitivity studies should identify the parameters that exert the greatest influence on critical engineering predictions.
Probabilistic analyses may use Monte Carlo simulation, Latin hypercube sampling, surrogate modelling, reliability methods or other appropriate uncertainty propagation techniques.
The software should report uncertainty intervals, reliability indicators and failure probabilities only to the extent supported by the modelling assumptions and available evidence.

Particular care is required when estimating rare structural failures, extreme environmental responses and long-term deterioration, because limited observations may not support precise probability estimates.
6. Validation documentation and traceability

Each suite should maintain a formal validation record identifying the model version, numerical method, calibration data, verification tests, validation datasets, acceptance criteria, discrepancies and applicable limitations.
Validation reports should distinguish test cases that passed, failed or remain untested.
A validated result should be linked to the particular software version, model configuration, physical assumptions and range of conditions for which supporting evidence exists.

Subsequent changes in numerical methods, material models, contact formulations, turbulence closures, fatigue models or coupled simulation workflows should trigger appropriate regression testing and, when necessary, renewed validation.
Recommended acceptance framework
The following classification can be used to track development and qualification of each engineering suite.
Classification
Required evidence
Implemented
Models and numerical methods are coded, with documented inputs, outputs and operating assumptions.
Calibration completed
Supported parameters have been fitted or identified using traceable measurement datasets.
Numerically verified
Appropriate analytical, benchmark, convergence, conservation and regression tests have passed.
Experimentally validated
Predictions agree with independent laboratory or physical-model measurements within defined acceptance criteria.
Field validated
Predictions agree with independent operational or full-scale field observations within defined conditions.
Integrated-system verified

Qualified for defined engineering use
Evidence supports a clearly specified application scope, with documented limitations and engineering acceptance criteria.

These classifications should be tracked separately where necessary: a suite may be validated for static strength but not for accidental impact, or for steady hydraulic flow but not for transient hydrate deposition.

Final engineering requirement: Each of the 17 suites should have its own documented calibration plan, verification test suite, independent validation matrix, uncertainty assessment, acceptance criteria and technical limitations. Industrial credibility should be established for each major physical capability and intended operating domain, rather than assigned automatically to the complete software application because selected benchmark cases passed.
geometry: Essential universal geometry-import capabilities for all 16 suites
A credible industrial software platform should implement a common geometry import architecture capable of processing the different geometry classes described above.

Exact CAD geometry: STEP, IGES, Parasolid and ACIS should be principal formats for high-fidelity mechanical geometry. STEP should be the preferred neutral exchange target for many precise 3D CAD interoperability workflows, while direct Parasolid and ACIS support may require compatible geometry kernels or licensed translators.

Structural and infrastructure geometry: IFC, SDNF, CIS/2, LandXML and compatible structural member descriptions should be supported as appropriate to the discipline. IFC should preserve available object identities, spatial relationships and material/section metadata, rather than treating every imported engineering assembly as an undifferentiated solid.

Surface and volume meshes: Gmsh MSH, Nastran BDF, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU, Exodus, CGNS, SU2 and OpenFOAM polyMesh should be handled through format-aware importers. Mesh element types, connectivity, boundary sets and physical groups must be checked before assignment to a solver.

Centreline and network geometry: CSV, XML, JSON, DXF polylines and geospatial vector formats should support three-dimensional routes, branches, connections, structural member centreline definitions, pipe profiles, riser configurations and cable/mooring arrangements. These imports should require an explicit schema or field mapping where their geometry definitions are not standardized.

Terrain, bathymetry and geospatial geometry: GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, LandXML, InfraGML, GML, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, Shapefile, XYZ, LAS/LAZ and suitable NetCDF datasets should be supported for surveyed and gridded seabed information. Coordinate reference systems, vertical datums and water-depth conventions require explicit handling.

Reconstructed, triangulated and point-cloud geometry: STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, 3MF, LAS/LAZ and E57 should support reverse engineering, scanning and nonparametric models. Surface meshes and point clouds must undergo the required reconstruction, repair, watertightness checks or mesh generation before they can be used in analyses that require solid or fluid domains.

For every imported geometry, the application should verify units, coordinate systems, scale, dimensional consistency, topological connectivity, missing faces, self-intersections, duplicate entities, nonmanifold edges, reversed surface normals, degeneracies and invalid structural connections.

The geometry processing system should support CAD healing, surface reconstruction, feature recognition, midsurface extraction, structural beam idealization, shell extraction, solid discretization, surface remeshing, volume meshing, local mesh refinement, material-region identification and suitable model simplification.

For assemblies, it should preserve component identities, relative positions, connection definitions, material associations and load-transfer interfaces wherever the source contains these data. It should also support mixed-representation models, such as structural beams connected to detailed shell models, pipeline centrelines positioned over surveyed bathymetry and floating bodies combined with mooring networks.

Important limitation: Not all listed file formats are directly interchangeable. Some are precise CAD formats, others are meshes, spatial datasets, drawings, point clouds or custom model descriptions. A universal application can offer broad import compatibility, but each format must have an implemented and tested reader and a defensible translation into the geometry representation required by the target analysis. Native proprietary files may require a license or the originating application's export functionality.

Recommended implementation: Use STEP/AP242 and compatible exact CAD representations for mechanical geometry, IFC for applicable structural/infrastructure models, industry-recognized mesh formats for finite-element and CFD discretizations, documented centreline schemas for pipelines/risers/moorings/cables, and geospatial/bathymetric formats for seabed geometry. This would provide a strong interoperability foundation across the 16 suites while allowing advanced formats to be added through validated adapters.
